title: How brand and interface should share one idea
metaTitle: Brand and UX alignment, one idea
excerpt: Brand and UX alignment means one idea survives from the homepage into the product. A quiet site and a loud app are an unfinished brand.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table. The shared table fits a piece about brand and interface decided together.
caption: The site and the product should be one conversation, not two moods. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What does it mean for brand and interface to share one idea?
faqs.answer: The homepage and the product should make the same promise in the same tone. Type, color, density, and the words on buttons come from one list. If the marketing site is quiet and the app is loud, visitors feel the break the moment they log in, and the brand is not finished.

faqs.question: Can a marketing site and a product look different?
faqs.answer: They can differ in layout, because a homepage and a tool have different jobs. They should not differ in the idea: the same type, the same accent, and the same kind of sentence. A campaign can be louder for a week, and the product should not inherit that volume by accident.

faqs.question: Who keeps the idea consistent?
faqs.answer: Whoever can refuse a new visual language. On a small team that is often one person across the site and the product, or a short shared page both sides use. Two vendors with two files will produce two brands unless the idea is written down and checked.

markdown:
Brand and UX alignment means one idea survives the trip from the homepage into the product. If the site is quiet and the app is loud, the brand is unfinished. People feel the break at the moment of login, which is a poor time to introduce a second company.

The idea does not have to be a slogan. It can be a behavior. This product is calm. This product is dense because traders need density. This product explains itself in one sentence. Whatever it is, the marketing page and the interface should be examples of it, not neighboring projects that share a logo.

## Name the idea in one sentence

Write the sentence before you debate components. We are a quiet place to read the work. We show only what changed and what needs a decision. We sound like a person, and the screen is mostly type. The sentence should be specific enough that a loud gradient and a calm manuscript cannot both satisfy it.

Hanabi's public line is clarity over complexity. On a site, that shows up as a readable page and an obvious way to talk. In a product interface, it shows up as fewer competing accents and words that say what happens next. Got Next and Leadly are public examples of product interfaces. Trade Moai is a trading interface concept organized around scanning. The shared lesson is focus. A marketing page for any of those products would have to feel like the same focus, or the portfolio would be two stories.

Test the sentence against a screen you already have. If the homepage satisfies it and the app does not, the app is where the work is. Buying a new homepage to cover an incoherent product only delays the moment people notice.

## What should match

Type should match in family and in manners, even when sizes differ. A display face on the homepage and a default system font in the product is a visible seam. You can use the system font. Then use it on the site too, or use the brand face in both places. The point is the relationship.

Color should match in roles, not only in a logo swatch. If accent means the one action on the site, accent means the one action in the product. A product that paints every button, badge, and chart in the accent has turned a signal into wallpaper. The site, if it was restrained, did not prepare anyone for that.

Density should match the idea. A calm brand with an interface crammed edge to edge is a contradiction. A tool for fast scanning with a marketing site full of huge empty statements may also be a contradiction, if the buyer came for the tool. Layouts can still differ. A homepage has a story. A dashboard has a job. The density of the type, the contrast, and the number of colors should feel decided by the same person.

Words should match. The noun for the thing the customer came for should be the same on the homepage, the navigation, and the empty state. Voice is part of alignment. A poetic site and a blunt product can work only if the bluntness is the idea and the poem was a mistake, or the reverse. Accidental contrast is not range. It is two authors.

## What can differ

The homepage can have a larger headline, a photograph, and a single story. The product can have tables, filters, and repeated days of use. Those are different jobs. Forcing the product to look like a campaign, or the campaign to look like a settings screen, makes both worse.

Motion can be richer on the site if it explains something, and quieter in the tool if people live there for hours. The idea still governs both. Motion that exists to impress, on a brand that claimed to be calm, is a break. So is a tool that animates every panel for a brand that claimed to respect time.

A campaign can raise its voice for a season. Give it an end date. When the campaign art becomes the product theme by default, you have let a poster repaint the interface. Bring the product back to the original idea, or change the idea on purpose and then change both.

## How the seam appears

The seam usually appears because two people worked in two files. A brand designer finishes a homepage. A product designer, or a framework theme, finishes the app. Each file is internally consistent. Together they are not. The logo in the corner is asked to do the work the decisions did not do.

Close the seam with a shared page: type, color roles, the sentence, and the components that repeat. The homepage and the app both use it. Hanabi designs and builds, which is one way the seam stays small. The people who set the brand are in the same work as the interface, using Figma where the structure is still moving and the codebase when the type and the states have to be real.

The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is a constraint both sides share, whether or not they share a taste. The guidelines sit under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Contrast, focus, and names for controls are not a separate brand. They are part of the idea that the product is usable. A beautiful site that hands people an interface they cannot operate has broken the promise in the most literal way.

## A review you can run in an hour

Open the homepage and the main product screen side by side.

- Does one sentence describe both?
- Are the type and the accent the same roles?
- Could the button labels have been written by the same person?
- Is the louder one loud for a reason you can say?

If you fail the first question, do not start a rebrand. Write the sentence, then change the screen that disagrees. Often that is a handful of colors and a pass on the words. A full visual reset is justified when the idea itself changed, which is a different decision from tidying a seam.

Components are how the idea survives the tenth screen, not only the first. [Component libraries that match the brand](/blog/components-that-match-the-brand) is the next piece, about why a default kit shows through and what to build instead.

When you want the site and the product to carry one idea, see [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful question in a portfolio is whether the interface and the brand look decided together.
